entity.name: Adam Smith
entity.description: The absent-minded professor who invented modern economics. A Scottish philosopher who got punished at Oxford for reading Hume, befriended Voltaire in Geneva and Benjamin Franklin in Paris, then went home to Kirkcaldy and spent ten years writing The Wealth of Nations. He ordered all his unpublished manuscripts burned before he died.

story.name: Adam Smith
story.description: A fatherless Scottish boy gets kidnapped by Romani at age three, suffers a nervous breakdown at Oxford, befriends Voltaire and Franklin across Europe, and publishes the book that invents modern economics.

moments.name: Adam Smith Is Born in Kirkcaldy to a Widowed Mother
moments.subtitle: A fatherless child who was briefly kidnapped by Romani at age three
moments.description: Adam Smith was baptized on 5 June 1723 in Kirkcaldy, Fife, Scotland — his actual birth date is unknown. His father, a senior solicitor and customs comptroller, had died two months before the birth. Raised entirely by his mother Margaret Douglas, the boy was reportedly kidnapped by Romani at age three and rescued shortly after. Smith attended Kirkcaldy's Burgh School, considered one of Scotland's best, from 1729 to 1737. He remained close to his mother his entire life, eventually moving back in with her in Edinburgh in 1778. The fatherless boy from a small Scottish town would become the most influential economist in history.

moments.name: Adam Smith Becomes Professor of Moral Philosophy at Glasgow
moments.subtitle: The 13 happiest years of his life, by his own account
moments.description: In 1752, Adam Smith was appointed Chair of Moral Philosophy at the University of Glasgow, a position he would hold for 12 years. Smith himself called this period "by far the most useful and therefore by far the happiest and most honorable" of his life. In 1759, he published The Theory of Moral Sentiments, which argued that human morality is rooted in sympathy — the capacity to feel what others feel. The book made him so famous that wealthy students left universities across Europe to study under him in Glasgow. In 1762, the university awarded him a Doctor of Laws degree, cementing his reputation as a leading Enlightenment thinker.

moments.name: Adam Smith Meets Voltaire During a European Grand Tour
moments.subtitle: Two Enlightenment titans discuss philosophy while Smith secretly drafts his masterwork
moments.description: In 1765, Adam Smith traveled to Geneva as tutor to the young Duke of Buccleuch and met the French philosopher Voltaire. Smith had resigned his Glasgow professorship in 1764 to take the tutoring position, which paid twice his academic salary plus a lifetime pension. Bored during a long stay in Toulouse, Smith had begun writing a book "to pass away the time" — the early drafts of what would become The Wealth of Nations. After Geneva, Smith moved to Paris, where he met Benjamin Franklin and the Physiocrat economists. These European encounters with radical economic thinkers crystallized Smith's arguments against mercantilism.

moments.name: Adam Smith Publishes The Wealth of Nations and Invents Modern Economics
moments.subtitle: A decade of solitary writing in a Scottish fishing town produces the most influential economics book ever
moments.description: On 9 March 1776, Adam Smith published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations in London. The first edition sold out in six months. Written over nearly ten years in his hometown of Kirkcaldy, the book demolished mercantilism and laid out the principles of free-market economics: division of labor, the "invisible hand" of self-interest driving public good, and the case against trade barriers. Published the same year as the American Declaration of Independence, it reshaped how governments thought about trade, taxation, and prosperity. Today it is considered the founding document of economics as an academic discipline.

moments.name: Adam Smith Dies After Ordering All His Unpublished Manuscripts Burned
moments.subtitle: The father of economics destroys 16 volumes of notes before anyone can read them
moments.description: On 17 July 1790, Adam Smith died at Panmure House in Edinburgh's Canongate at the age of 67. Before his death, Smith ordered his executors to burn 16 volumes of unpublished manuscripts — an act that has tormented scholars ever since, as the destroyed works may have included a promised treatise on jurisprudence. Smith had spent his final years as Commissioner of Customs in Scotland, living with his elderly mother until her death in 1784. He was buried in the Canongate Kirkyard. The man who explained how markets create wealth died having given away most of his income to secret charitable causes during his lifetime.
